abstract: The outcomes implied by a survey of US adults of the Anthropic Institute's task-based model of AI's economic effects to 2030 (Korinek, Jones, Sacher, Cotter and McCrory, Working Paper 2026-02). Parameters: each respondent's own five answers, with reinstatement, posting speed, wage rigidity and capital supply elasticity held at the substantial scenario's values. The model maps these into paths for GDP, the labor share, wages, labor reallocation and unemployment.
keyFindings: Morning Consult surveyed 10,980 US adults on August 11-23 2026 about AI capabilities, adoption, autonomy, productivity gains and re-employment time. Median implied parameters were an affected mass of 0.44, diffusion 0.40, automation share 0.47, gain 0.44 in logs and a search discount of 0.064.

Running the 3,259 respondents who answered all five items through the model gives a median cognitive employment change of -4.2 percent since mid-2026, with an interquartile range of -9 to -1 percent - the only figure in the paper that is a central tendency with a stated dispersion rather than an unweighted illustration.

Other median implied outcomes: GDP 8.6 percent above the no-AI path [3, 19], the average wage 2.6 percent above it [0, 13], cognitive unemployment 4.6 percent [3, 8] and all-worker unemployment 4.6 percent [4, 6]. The public's expectations land close to the substantial change scenario.
methodology: Task-based computational model calibrated to mid-2026 baseline using CPS employment data (cognitive occupations comprise 62.4 percent of employment) and Census BTOS data on AI adoption (18 percent of firms, 32 percent employment-weighted in late 2025). Three scenarios parameterized by five AI-related objects (task mass, diffusion, productivity gain, automation share, reinstatement ratio) and two labor-market frictions (search discount, posting speed). Survey component: 10,980 US adults surveyed via Morning Consult August 11-23, 2026, on five items regarding AI capability timelines, task coverage, speed gains, augmentation versus automation, and job search duration. Respondent parameters (n=3,259 completing all items) run through the model to generate predicted outcomes with interquartile ranges.
qualifiers: The scenarios are not predictions and no probabilities are attached. The framework omits catastrophic risks, political economy, business cycles, financial market disruptions, price rigidities and associated demand effects, AI in household production, and data-center buildout effects. Worker heterogeneity is very coarse—workers differ only by employment status and occupation group, with displaced workers earning the destination wage immediately with no tenure discount. The model does not follow individual workers and considers only cognitive tasks, excluding rapid robotics advances, which is why analysis stops at 2030. External reviewers (including Acemoglu, Autor, Moll, Nakamura, Restrepo, Romer, Steinsson) were not asked to endorse conclusions. Some reviewers questioned whether exposed occupations will shrink at all, whether the extreme scenario is overstated as a thought experiment, and whether the modest scenario understates current observable trends.
